*Text-critical note:* For the MT reading וַיֵּלֶךְ (vayyelekh, “he went”), the LXX and Qumran have וַיְכַל (vayekhal, “he finished”): “So Moses finished speaking,” etc. The difficult reading of the MT favors its authenticity.

*Translator's note:* In the MT this refers to the words that follow (cf. NIV, NCV).
*Translator's note:* Or “am no longer able to lead you” (NIV, NLT); *Heb* “am no longer able to go out and come in.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “and said to him.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fathers” (also in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:20|20}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Moses.” The pronoun has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term שְׁמִטָּה (shemittah), a derivative of the verb שָׁמַט (shamat, “to release; to relinquish”), refers to the procedure whereby debts of all fellow Israelites were to be canceled. Since the Feast of Tabernacles celebrated God’s own deliverance of and provision for his people, this was an appropriate time for Israelites to release one another. See note on this word at {{Deuteronomy 15:1|Deut 15:1}}.

*Study note:* For the regulations on this annual festival see {{Deuteronomy 16:13|Deut 16:13-15}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew phrase חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת (khag hassukkot, “festival of huts” [or “shelters”]) is traditionally known as the Feast of Tabernacles. See note on the name of the festival in {{Deuteronomy 16:13|Deut 16:13}}.

*Study note:* The ger (גֵּר) “foreign resident” or “naturalized citizen,” (see {{Exodus 12:19|Exod 12:19}} and {{Deuteronomy 29:10|Deut 29:10-13}}) could make sacrifices (Lev 17:8; 22:18; {{Numbers 15:14|Num 15:14}}) and participate in Israel’s religious festivals: Passover {{Exodus 12:48|Exod 12:48}}; Day of Atonement Lev 16:29; Feast of Weeks {{Deuteronomy 16:10|Deut 16:10-14}}; Feast of Tabernacles/Temporary Shelters {{Deuteronomy 31:12|Deut 31:12}}.

*Translator's note:* The phrase “this law” is not in the Hebrew text, but English style requires an object for the verb here. Other translations also supply the object which is otherwise implicit (cf. NIV “who do not know this law”; TEV “who have never heard the Law of the Lord your God”).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads “by the door of the tent” in line with v. {{Deuteronomy 31:10|10}} but also, perhaps, as a reflection of its tendency to avoid over-familiarity with Yahweh and his transcendence.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “tent of assembly” (אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, ʾohel moʿed); this is not always the same as the tabernacle, which is usually called מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan, “dwelling-place”), a reference to its being invested with God’s presence. The “tent of meeting” was erected earlier than the tabernacle and was the place where Yahweh occasionally appeared, especially to Moses (cf. {{Exodus 18:7|Exod 18:7-16}}; {{Exodus 33:7|33:7-11}}; {{Numbers 11:16|Num 11:16}}, {{Numbers 11:24|24}}, {{Numbers 11:26|26}}; {{Numbers 12:4|12:4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will command him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the pillar of cloud.” This phrase was not repeated in the translation; a relative clause was used instead.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lie down with your fathers” (so NASB); NRSV “ancestors.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.” Smr, LXX, and the Targums read the plural “they,” which is necessary in any case in the translation because of contemporary English style. The third person singular also occurs in the Hebrew text twice more in this verse, three times in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:17|17}}, once in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:18|18}}, five times in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:20|20}}, and four times in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:21|21}}. Each time it is translated as third person plural for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.” Smr, LXX, and the Targums read the plural “they.” See note on the first occurrence of “they” in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:16|16}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “abandon” (TEV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on that day.” This same expression also appears later in the verse and in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:18|18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him.” Smr, LXX, and the Targums read the plural “them.” See note on the first occurrence of “they” in v. {{Deuteronomy 31:16|16}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.” Since the pronoun could be taken to refer to Moses, the referent has been specified as “the Lord” in the translation for clarity. See also the note on the word “you” later in this verse.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads, “as the Lord promised them, and he will be with you.” This relieves the problem of Moses apparently promising to be with Joshua as the MT reads on the surface (“I will be with you”). However, the reading of the LXX is clearly an attempt to clarify an existing obscurity and therefore is unlikely to reflect the original.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Moses.” The pronoun has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stiffness of neck” (cf. KJV, NAB, NIV). See note on the word “stubborn” in {{Deuteronomy 9:6|Deut 9:6}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “How much more after my death?” The Hebrew text has a sarcastic rhetorical question here; the translation seeks to bring out the force of the question.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates with “totally.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do the evil.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of your hands.”
*Translator's note:* Or “mist,” “light drizzle.” In some contexts the term appears to refer to light rain, rather than dew.
*Text-critical note:* Smr and Tg read “in the name.”

*Study note:* The Hebrew term depicts God as a rocky summit where one may find safety and protection. Within a covenantal context it serves as a reminder to the people that their God has committed himself to their protection in return for their allegiance.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads Θεός (theos, “God”) for the MT’s “Rock.”

*Translator's note:* Or “just” (KJV, NAB, NRSV, NLT) or “righteous” (NASB).

*Text-critical note:* The third person masculine singular שָׁחַת (shakhat) is rendered as third person masculine plural by Smr, a reading supported by the plural suffix on מוּם (mum, “defect”) as well as the plural of בֵּן (ben, “sons”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “have acted corruptly” (so NASB, NIV84, NLT); NRSV “have dealt falsely.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “(they are) not his sons.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “defect” (so NASB). This highly elliptical line suggests that Israel’s major fault was its failure to act like God’s people; in fact, they acted quite the contrary.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “twisted,” “crooked.” See {{Psalm 18:26|Ps 18:26}}.

*Text-critical note:* The Syriac, Targum, and Vulgate read second person masculine singular whereas the MT has second person masculine plural. The former is preferred, the latter perhaps being a misreading (בִּינוּ [binu] for בִּינָה [binah]). Both the preceding (“remember”) and following (“ask”) imperatives are singular forms in the Hebrew text.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “generation and generation.” The repetition of the singular noun here singles out each of the successive past generations. See *IBHS* 116 §7.2.3b.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term עֶלְיוֹן (ʿelyon) is an abbreviated form of the divine name *El Elyon*, frequently translated “God Most High” (so here NCV, CEV) or something similar. This full name (or epithet) occurs only in {{Genesis 14|Gen 14}}, though the two elements are parallel in {{Psalm 73:11|Pss 73:11}}; {{Psalm 107:11|107:11}}; etc. Here it is clear that Elyon has to do with the nations in general whereas in v. {{Deuteronomy 32:9|9}}, by contrast, Yahweh relates specifically to Israel. See T. Fretheim, *NIDOTTE* 1:400-401. The title depicts God as the sovereign ruler of the world, who is enthroned high above his dominion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sons of man” (so NASB); or “the sons of Adam” (so KJV).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “the sons of Israel.” The idea, perhaps, is that Israel was central to Yahweh’s purposes and all other nations were arranged and distributed according to how they related to Israel. See S. R. Driver, *Deuteronomy* (ICC), 355-56. For the MT בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (bene yisraʾel, “sons of Israel”) a Qumran fragment has “sons of God,” while the LXX reads ἀγγέλων θεοῦ (angelōn theou, “angels of God”), presupposing בְּנֵי אֵל (bene ʾel) or בְּנֵי אֵלִים (bene ʾelim). “Sons of God” is undoubtedly the original reading; the MT and LXX have each interpreted it differently. MT assumes that the expression “sons of God” refers to Israel (cf. Hos. 1:10), while LXX has assumed that the phrase refers to the angelic heavenly assembly ({{Psalm 29:1|Pss 29:1}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}; cf. as well {{Psalm 82|Ps 82}}). The phrase is also attested in Ugaritic, where it refers to the high god El’s divine assembly. According to the latter view, which is reflected in the translation, the Lord delegated jurisdiction over the nations to his angelic host (cf. Dan. 10:13-21), while reserving for himself Israel, over whom he rules directly. For a defense of the view taken here, see M. S. Heiser, “{{Deuteronomy 32:8|Deuteronomy 32:8}} and the Sons of God,” *BSac* 158 (2001): 52-74.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “the portion of his inheritance.” The LXX and Smr add “Israel” and *BHS* suggests the reconstruction: “The Lord’s allotment is Jacob, the portion of his inheritance is Israel” (cf. NAB). While providing good parallelism, it destroys a fine chiastic structure: “allotment” (a), “his people” (b), “Jacob (b’), and “inheritance” (a’).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.” The referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The reference is to “his people/Jacob” (cf. v. {{Deuteronomy 32:9|9}}), that is, Israel (using a collective singular). The singular pronouns are replaced by plural ones throughout vv. {{Deuteronomy 32:10|10-14}} by some English versions as an aid to the modern reader (cf. NAB, NCV, TEV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a land of wilderness.” A מִדְבָּר (midbar, “wilderness”) refers to a dry region which is characterized as receiving less than twelve inches of rain per year. It therefore cannot support trees and may or may not have sparse vegetation (if receiving less than six inches of rain). The point of the poetic image is that it is desolate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in an empty, howling wasteland.” The word “howling” is derived from a verbal root that typically refers to the wailing of mourners. Here it likely refers to the howling of desert animals, or perhaps to the howling wind, in which case one may translate, “in an empty, windy wasteland.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “was surrounding him.” The distinctive form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is an imperfect, not a preterite. As such it draws attention to God’s continuing care during the period in view. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” *Hebrew Studies* 27 (1986): 15-16.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he gave him understanding.” The form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is a preterite, not an imperfect. As such it simply states the action factually. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” *Hebrew Studies* 27 (1986): 15-16.

*Translator's note:* The distinctive form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is an imperfect, not a preterite. As such it draws attention to God’s continuing protection during the period in view. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” *Hebrew Studies* 27 (1986): 15-16.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the little man.” The term אִישׁוֹן (ʾishon) means literally “little man,” perhaps because when one looks into another’s eyes he sees himself reflected there in miniature. See A. Harman, *NIDOTTE* 1:391.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is an imperfect, indicating habitual or typical behavior. The parallel verb (cf. “hovers” in the next line) is used in the same manner.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The form of the suffix on this and the following verb forms (cf. “lifted him up”) indicates that the verbs are preterites, not imperfects. As such they simply state the action factually. The use of the preterite here suggests that the preceding verb (cf. “spread out”) is preterite as well.

*Translator's note:* The distinctive form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is an imperfect, not a preterite. As such it draws attention to God’s continuing guidance during the period in view.

*Translator's note:* The form of the suffix on this verbal form indicates that the verb is a preterite, not an imperfect. As such it simply states the action factually. Note as well the preterites with vav (ו) consecutive that follow in the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he made him suck honey from the rock.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “oil,” but this probably refers to olive oil; see note on the word “rock” at the end of this verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “flinty.”

*Study note:* *Olive oil* from *rock* probably suggests olive trees growing on rocky ledges and yet doing so productively. See E. H. Merrill, *Deuteronomy* (NAC), 415; cf. TEV “their olive trees flourished in stony ground.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blood,” a figurative image based on the color of the juice.

*Translator's note:* To make the continuity of the referent clear, some English versions substitute “Jacob” here (NAB, NRSV) while others replace “Jeshurun” with “Israel” (NCV, CEV, NLT) or “the Lord’s people” (TEV).

*Study note:* *Jeshurun* is a term of affection derived from the Hebrew verb יָשַׁר (yashar, “be upright”). Here it speaks of Israel “in an ideal situation, with its ‘uprightness’ due more to God’s help than his own efforts” (M. Mulder, *TDOT* 6:475).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads the third person masculine singular (“he”) for the MT second person masculine singular (“you”), but such alterations are unnecessary in Hebrew poetic texts where subjects fluctuate frequently and without warning.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “with strange (things).” The Vulgate actually supplies *diis* (“gods”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “abhorrent (things)” (cf. NRSV). A number of English versions understand this as referring to “idols” (NAB, NIV, NCV, CEV), while NLT supplies “acts.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text is uncertain here; the translation follows the suggestion offered in *HALOT* 1477 s.v. שׁיה. Cf. NASB, NLT “You neglected”; NIV “You deserted”; NRSV “You were unmindful of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will hide my face from them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons” (so NAB, NASB); TEV “unfaithful people.”

*Study note:* *They have made me jealous*. The “jealousy” of God is not a spirit of pettiness prompted by his insecurity, but righteous indignation caused by the disloyalty of his people to his covenant grace (see note on the word “God” in {{Deuteronomy 4:24|Deut 4:24}}). The jealousy of Israel, however (see next line), will be envy because of God’s lavish attention to another nation. This is an ironic wordplay. See H. Peels, *NIDOTTE* 3:938-39.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what is not a god,” or a “nondeity.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their empty (things).” The Hebrew term used here to refer pejoratively to the false gods is הֶבֶל (hevel, “futile” or “futility”), used frequently in Ecclesiastes (e.g., Eccl 1:1, “Futile! Futile!” laments the Teacher, “Absolutely futile! Everything is futile!”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what is not a people,” or a “nonpeople.” The “nonpeople” (לֹא־עָם, loʾ ʿam) referred to here are Gentiles who someday would become God’s people in the fullest sense (cf. Hos 1:9; 2:23).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a foolish nation” (so KJV, NAB, NRSV); NIV “a nation that has no understanding”; NLT “I will provoke their fury by blessing the foolish Gentiles.”

*Study note:* *Sheol* refers here not to hell and hell-fire—a much later concept—but to the innermost parts of the earth, as low down as one could get. The parallel with “the foundations of the mountains” makes this clear (cf. {{Psalm 9:17|Pss 9:17}}; {{Psalm 16:10|16:10}}; {{Psalm 139:8|139:8}}; {{Isaiah 14:9|Isa 14:9}}, {{Isaiah 14:15|15}}; {{Amos 9:2|Amos 9:2}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “to the lowest depths of the earth”; cf. NAB “to the depths of the nether world”; NIV11 “to the realm of the dead below”; NLT “to the depths of the grave.”
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term קֶטֶב (qetev) is probably metaphorical here for the sting of a disease (*HALOT* 1091-92 s.v.).
*Translator's note:* A verb is omitted here in the Hebrew text; for purposes of English style one suitable to the context is supplied.
*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads “I said I would scatter them.” This reading is followed by a number of English versions (e.g., KJV, ASV, NIV, NCV, NRSV, NLT, CEV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “anger.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Our hand is high.” Cf. NAB “Our own hand won the victory.”

*Translator's note:* The words “man” and “of them” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sold them” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their,” but the referent (enemies) is specified in the translation for the sake of clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “vine.”

*Study note:* *Sodom…Gomorrah*. The term “vine” is a reference to the pagan deities which, the passage says, find their ultimate source in Sodom and Gomorrah, that is, in the soil of perversion exemplified by these places (cf. {{Genesis 18:20|Gen 18:20}}; {{Genesis 19:4|19:4-28}}; {{Isaiah 1:10|Isa 1:10}}; {{Isaiah 3:9|3:9}}; Jer 23:14; Lam 4:6; {{Ezekiel 16:44|Ezek 16:44-52}}; {{Matthew 10:15|Matt 10:15}}; 11:23-24).
*Translator's note:* Verses {{Deuteronomy 32:34|34-35}} appear to be a quotation of the Lord and so the introductory phrase “says the Lord” is supplied in the translation.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “prepared things,” “impending things.” See BDB 800 s.v. עָתִיד.

*Translator's note:* The translation understands the verb in the sense of “be grieved, relent” (cf. *HALOT* 689 s.v. נחם hitp 2); cf. KJV, ASV “repent himself”; NLT “will change his mind”; NIV11 “relent.” Another option is to translate “will show compassion to” (see BDB 637 s.v. נחם); cf. NASB, NIV84, NRSV.

*Translator's note:* Verses {{Deuteronomy 32:39|39-42}} appear to be a quotation of the Lord and so the introductory phrase “says the Lord” is supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “deliver from” (so NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “judgment.” This is a metonymy, a figure of speech in which the effect (judgment) is employed as an instrument (sword, spear, or the like), the means, by which it is brought about.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term שָׂנֵא (saneʾ, “hate”) in this covenant context speaks of those who reject Yahweh’s covenant overtures, that is, who disobey its stipulations (see note on the word “rejecting” in {{Deuteronomy 5:9|Deut 5:9}}; also see {{Deuteronomy 7:10|Deut 7:10}}; 2 Chr 19:2; {{Psalm 81:15|Pss 81:15}}; {{Psalm 139:20|139:20-21}}).
*Translator's note:* Or “head” (the same Hebrew word can mean “head” in the sense of “leader, chieftain” or “head” in the sense of body part).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Hoshea” (so KJV, ASV), another name for the same individual (cf. {{Numbers 13:8|Num 13:8}}, {{Numbers 13:16|16}}).

*Study note:* *Abarim*. This refers to the high plateau region of the Transjordan, the highest elevation of which is Mount Pisgah (or Nebo; cf. {{Deuteronomy 34:1|Deut 34:1}}). See also the note on the name “Pisgah” in {{Deuteronomy 3:17|Deut 3:17}}.

*Translator's note:* In the Hebrew text the forms translated “you will die…and join” are imperatives, but the actions in view cannot really be commanded. The imperative is used here in a rhetorical, emphatic manner to indicate the certainty of Moses’ death on the mountain. On the rhetorical use of the imperative see *IBHS* 572 §34.4c.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be gathered to your people.” The same phrase occurs again later in this verse.

*Study note:* *Mount Hor*. See note on the name “Moserah” in {{Deuteronomy 10:6|Deut 10:6}}.

*Translator's note:* The use of the plural (“you”) in the Hebrew text suggests that Moses and Aaron are both in view here, since both had rebelled at some time or other, if not at Meribah Kadesh then elsewhere (cf. {{Numbers 20:24|Num 20:24}}; {{Numbers 27:14|27:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not esteem me holy.” Cf. NIV “did not uphold my holiness”; NLT “failed to demonstrate my holiness.”

*Translator's note:* Or “rose like the sun” (NCV, TEV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (Israel) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “to him.” The LXX reads “to us” (לָנוּ [lanu] for לָמוֹ [lamo]), the reading of the MT is acceptable since it no doubt has in mind Israel as a collective singular.

*Translator's note:* Or “he shone forth” (NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Text-critical note:* With slight alteration (מִמְרִבַת קָדֵשׁ [mimrivat qadesh] for the MT’s מֵרִבְבֹת קֹדֶשׁ [merivevot qodesh]) the translation would be “from Meribah Kadesh” (cf. NAB, NLT; see {{Deuteronomy 32:51|Deut 32:51}}). However, the language of holy war in the immediate context favors the reading of the MT, which views the Lord as accompanied by angelic hosts.

*Text-critical note:* The mispointed Hebrew term אֵשְׁדָּת (ʾeshdat) should perhaps be construed as אֵשְׁהַת (ʾeshhat) with Smr.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “peoples.” The apparent plural form is probably a misunderstood singular (perhaps with a pronominal suffix) with enclitic mem (ם). See *HALOT* 838 s.v. עַם B.2.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “his holy ones.” The third person masculine singular suffix of the Hebrew MT is problematic in light of the second person masculine singular suffix on בְּיָדֶךָ (beyadekha, “your hands”). The LXX versions by Lucian and Origen read, therefore, “the holy ones.” The LXX version by Theodotion and the Vulgate, however, presuppose third masculine singular suffix on בְּיָדָיו (beyadayv, “his hands”), and thus retain “his holy ones.” The efforts to bring pronominal harmony into the line is commendable but unnecessary given the Hebrew tendency to be untroubled by such grammatical inconsistencies. However, the translation harmonizes the first pronoun with the second so that the referent (the Lord) is clear.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hands.” For the problem of the pronoun see note on the term “holy ones” earlier in this verse.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term תֻּכּוּ (tukku, probably Pual perfect of תָּכָה, takhah) is otherwise unknown. The present translation is based on the reference to feet and, apparently, receiving instruction in God’s words (cf. KJV, ASV). Other options are as follows: NIV “At your feet they all bow down” (cf. NCV, CEV); NLT “They follow in your steps” (cf. NAB, NASB); NRSV “they marched at your heels.”

*Translator's note:* The singular verbal form in the Hebrew text (lit. “he lifts up”) is understood in a distributive manner, focusing on the action of each individual within the group.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term תּוֹרָה (torah) here should be understood more broadly as instruction.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he was king.” The present translation avoids the sudden shift in person and the mistaken impression that Moses is the referent by specifying the referent as “the Lord.”

*Study note:* *Jeshurun* is a term of affection referring to Israel, derived from the Hebrew verb יָשַׁר (yashar, “be upright”). See note on the term in {{Deuteronomy 32:15|Deut 32:15}}.

*Study note:* The following blessing is given to the tribes in order, although the tribe of Simeon is curiously missing from the list.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [not] may his men be few” (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV).
*Translator's note:* The words “the blessing” are supplied in the translation for clarity and stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* *Thummim and Urim*. These terms, whose meaning is uncertain, refer to sacred stones carried in a pouch on the breastplate of the high priest and examined on occasion as a means of ascertaining God’s will or direction. See {{Exodus 28:30|Exod 28:30}}; Lev 8:8; {{Numbers 27:21|Num 27:21}}; {{1 Samuel 28:6|1 Sam 28:6}}. See also C. Van Dam, *NIDOTTE* 1:329-31.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “godly man.” The reference is probably to Moses as representative of the whole tribe of Levi.

*Study note:* *Massah* means “testing” in Hebrew; the name is a wordplay on what took place there. Cf. {{Exodus 17:7|Exod 17:7}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:16|Deut 6:16}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:22|9:22}}; {{Psalm 95:8|Ps 95:8-9}}.

*Study note:* *Meribah* means “contention, argument” in Hebrew; this is another wordplay on the incident that took place there. Cf. {{Numbers 20:13|Num 20:13}}, {{Numbers 20:24|24}}; {{Psalm 106:32|Ps 106:32}}.
*Study note:* This statement no doubt alludes to the Levites’ destruction of their own fellow tribesmen following the golden calf incident ({{Exodus 32:25|Exod 32:25-29}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “smash the sinews [or “loins,” so many English versions].” This part of the body was considered to be center of one’s strength (cf. {{Job 40:16|Job 40:16}}; {{Psalm 69:24|Ps 69:24}}; {{Proverbs 31:17|Prov 31:17}}; Nah 2:2, 11). See J. H. Tigay, *Deuteronomy* (JPSTC), 325.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “between his shoulders.” This suggests the scene in {{John 13:23|John 13:23}} with Jesus and the Beloved Disciple.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the harvest of the heavens.” The referent appears to be good crops produced by the rain that falls from the sky.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “goings forth of the sun.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from the harvest of the yield of.” This has been simplified in the translation to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the moon.” Many English versions regard this as a reference to “months” (“moons”) rather than the moon itself (cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* The expression “him who resided in the bush” is frequently understood as a reference to the appearance of the Lord to Moses at Sinai from a burning bush (so NIV, NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT; cf. {{Exodus 2:2|Exod 2:2-6}}; {{Exodus 3:2|3:2}}, {{Exodus 3:4|4}}). To make this reference clear the word “burning” is supplied in the translation.

*Study note:* This apparently refers to Joseph’s special status among his brothers as a result of his being chosen by God to save the family from the famine and to lead Egypt.

*Study note:* *Ephraim* and *Manasseh* were the sons of Joseph who became founders of the two tribes into which Joseph’s descendants were split ({{Genesis 48:19|Gen 48:19-20}}). Jacob’s blessing granted favored status to Ephraim; this is probably why Ephraim is viewed here as more numerous than Manasseh.

*Translator's note:* Or “acceptable”; *Heb* “righteous” (so NASB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “suck.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of the sand” (so NRSV, NLT); CEV “the sandy beach.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term מְחֹקֵק (mekhoqeq; Poel participle of חָקַק, khaqaq, “to inscribe”) reflects the idea that the recorder of allotments (the “ruler”) is able to set aside for himself the largest and best. See E. H. Merrill, *Deuteronomy* (NAC), 444-45.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “covered in” (if from the root סָפַן, safan; cf. *HALOT* 764-65 s.v. ספן qal).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heads” (in the sense of chieftains).
*Study note:* *He will leap forth from Bashan*. This may refer to Dan’s conquest of Laish, a region just to the west of Bashan ({{Judges 18:27|Judg 18:27-28}}).

*Study note:* *Dip his foot in olive oil*. This is a metaphor for prosperity, one especially apt in light of the abundance of olive groves in the area settled by Asher. The Hebrew term refers to olive oil, which symbolizes blessing in the OT. See R. Way, *NIDOTTE* 4:171-73.
*Translator's note:* The words “of your gates” have been supplied in the translation to clarify the referent of “bars.”

*Study note:* *Jeshurun* is a term of affection referring to Israel, derived from the Hebrew verb יָשַׁר (yashar, “be upright”). See note on the term in {{Deuteronomy 32:15|Deut 32:15}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “(who) rides (on) the heavens” (cf. NIV, NRSV, NLT). This title depicts Israel’s God as sovereign over the elements of the storm (cf. {{Psalm 68:33|Ps 68:33}}). The use of the phrase here may be polemical; Moses may be asserting that Israel’s God, not Baal (called the “rider of the clouds” in the Ugaritic myths), is the true divine king (cf. v. {{Deuteronomy 33:5|5}}) who controls the elements of the storm, grants agricultural prosperity, and delivers his people from their enemies. See R. B. Chisholm, Jr., “The Polemic against Baalism in Israel’s Early History and Literature,” *BSac* 151 (1994): 275.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from under, arms of perpetuity.” The words “you” and “his” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Some have perceived this line to be problematic and have offered alternative translations that differ significantly from the present translation: “He spread out the primeval tent; he extended the ancient canopy” (NAB); “He subdues the ancient gods, shatters the forces of old” (NRSV). These are based on alternate meanings or conjectural emendations rather than textual variants in the mss and versions.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all alone.” The idea is that such vital resources as water will some day no longer need protection because God will provide security.

*Translator's note:* Or “skies.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “drizzle, showers.” See note at {{Deuteronomy 32:2|Deut 32:2}}.
*Study note:* For the geography involved, see note on the term “Pisgah” in {{Deuteronomy 3:17|Deut 3:17}} and the note on “rift valley plains” in {{Numbers 22:1|Num 22:1}}.
*Translator's note:* Or “western” (so NAB, NASB, NIV84, NRSV); *Heb* “latter,” a reference to the Mediterranean Sea (cf. NCV, TEV, CEV, NIV11, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seed” (so KJV, ASV).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “with your eyes,” but this is redundant in English and is left untranslated.

*Text-critical note:* Smr and some LXX mss read “they buried him,” that is, the Israelites. The MT reads “he buried him,” meaning in the context that “the Lord buried him.” This understanding, combined with the statement at the end of the verse that Moses’ burial place is unknown, gave rise to traditions during the intertestamental period that are reflected in the NT in {{Judges 9|Jude 9}} and in OT pseudepigraphic works like the *Assumption of Moses*.

*Translator's note:* Or “dimmed.” The term could refer to dull appearance or to dimness caused by some loss of visual acuity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sap.” That is, he was still in possession of his faculties or liveliness.
*Study note:* This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at {{Numbers 22:1|Num 22:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to,” “with respect to.” In the Hebrew text vv. {{Deuteronomy 34:10|10-12}} are one long sentence. For stylistic reasons the translation divides this into two, using the verb “he did” at the beginning of v. {{Deuteronomy 34:11|11}} and “he displayed” at the beginning of v. {{Deuteronomy 34:12|12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “strong hand.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text of v. {{Deuteronomy 34:12|12}} reads literally, “with respect to all the strong hand and with respect to all the awesome greatness which Moses did before the eyes of all Israel.”
